title: Labels do not share words or roots with the text on their own page: a meaning-linked prediction fails before anyone builds a language for it
statement: P-G-006 asks for a constructed language whose meaning-linked predictions include 'labels share roots with the text about the same object'. Measured first on all public pages (practice training and evaluation; ZL, certain words, the 39 pages that have both labels and paragraph text: herbal 5, cosmological 3, astronomical 3, zodiac 0, biological 11, pharmaceutical 15, text 2). For each label word I asked whether the paragraph text of its own page holds the same word, a word one glyph edit away, or a word with the same first three or four glyphs, and compared with the paragraph text of a random other page of the same section (199 draws). Same word, labels of 3+ glyphs (531): 0.094 own page against 0.088 other pages. Same or one glyph away: 0.350 against 0.332 (labels of 3+), 0.224 against 0.216 (5+). Same first three glyphs (labels of 5+, 397): 0.494 against 0.489, p = 0.44; first four (6+, 272): 0.272 against 0.262, p = 0.37. So a label is no more likely to be found, whole or by its opening glyphs, in the text beside it than in the text of another page of its section; whatever ties labels to their pages (P-L4 work, M-L2's jar against plant-part contrast), it is not shared vocabulary with the paragraph. Implications: an invented-language attack should not register this prediction as a fact, since it is already false on public pages; a language in which labels name the drawn object and the paragraph describes it would have to use different words for the object in the two places, which is a strong and odd constraint; and nothing here distinguishes language from a meaningless procedure, since a procedure that writes labels from a separate table predicts the same null. Limits: roots taken as opening glyphs only, no allowance for prefixes such as o-, qo- or ch- that may be grammatical; a test that strips them is the next step.
check: Rerun on public pages: for each certain label word, look up its own page's paragraph text against other pages of the same section, by whole word, one-glyph edit, and shared opening glyphs; then repeat with common opening prefixes (o, qo, ch, sh, d) stripped.
